articles.title: Germany shifts toward tougher EU trade defenses as pressure from Chinese competition grows - DW.com
articles.summary: Germany shifts toward tougher EU trade defenses as pressure from Chinese competition grows  DW.com
articles.full_text:
Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.
Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
The cost of standing still
Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."
Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.
Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.
Why Berlin's China policy is changing
German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.
Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.
In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.
"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Industry pressure grows for trade defenses
Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.
While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."
Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.
Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.
EU weighs additional trade measures
Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.
Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.
Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.
MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.
Edited by: Tim Rooks

articles.title: France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation - The Guardian
articles.summary: France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation  The GuardianFrance and Germany to allow UK to join EU car policy if it aligns on China tariffs  Financial TimesAuto Industry Warns Brussels Against Locking Britain Out  ImpakterBritain shouldn’t rush in to EU’s battle against Chinese competition  The ObserverUK could be allowed to join EU car policy  Breakingthenews.net
articles.full_text:
France has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs.
In a breakthrough for Andy Burnham, France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition.
According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe.
“For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i.e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020.
It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU.
The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised with China on its exports of hybrid cars.
The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing.
“Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said.
“Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.”
On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package.
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said.
The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs.
He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”.
A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”

articles.title: UK weighs alignment with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs, raising stakes for global auto trade - Business Upturn
articles.summary: UK weighs alignment with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs, raising stakes for global auto trade  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Britain is considering whether to align its import duties on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) with the European Union, as London seeks to protect its automotive manufacturing interests and maintain access to European industrial support. The issue was highlighted in a POLITICO report published on October 7, 2026, following discussions between UK Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds and EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič. The UK government has not announced a final decision to impose tariffs.
The discussions reflect a wider trade-policy dilemma: Britain wants to preserve affordable EV choices and Chinese investment while ensuring UK-made vehicles remain competitive within European supply chains. EU officials have linked closer trade-policy alignment to proposals that could give European manufacturers preferential access to public procurement, subsidies and other industrial support.
Why Britain is considering a policy shift
The EU imposed additional countervailing duties on Chinese battery electric vehicles in October 2024 following an investigation into state subsidies. The duties vary by manufacturer and can reach 35% on top of the EU’s standard 10% car import tariff. Britain, by contrast, has not introduced equivalent additional tariffs specifically targeting Chinese EVs.
The UK’s position is complicated by its close automotive links with Europe. Different manufacturers have competing interests over tariffs, prices, investment and access to export markets. The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders has warned that trade restrictions should be based on robust evidence and account for the interests of consumers, manufacturers and exporters.
What the development means for India
For India, the debate offers a signal of how major markets are reassessing competition from Chinese EV manufacturers. Indian automakers and component suppliers seeking to expand exports to Britain and Europe will need to monitor changing import duties, sourcing requirements and incentives for locally manufactured vehicles.
Higher tariffs could make some Chinese-made EVs less price-competitive in Britain, potentially creating room for other suppliers. However, Indian manufacturers would not automatically benefit: their competitiveness would still depend on vehicle pricing, product quality, battery technology, regulatory compliance and distribution networks.
A UK move towards EU-style tariffs could also complicate Chinese automakers’ international expansion strategies and influence decisions about manufacturing plants and supply chains. For Indian companies, the broader lesson is that access to overseas markets increasingly depends on trade policy as well as manufacturing costs.
What happens next?
UK officials are expected to continue consultations with industry and discussions with Brussels. The government has said its approach will reflect the UK’s national interests, and no final tariff decision has been confirmed. Any policy change would require further details on the products covered, tariff rates and implementation arrangements.
5 key highlights
- Britain is reviewing potential tariffs on Chinese electric vehicle imports.
- EU alignment could affect access to European industrial support.
- UK manufacturers remain divided over the costs and benefits.
- Indian exporters are watching changes in global EV competition.
- London has not confirmed a final tariff decision.

articles.summary: EU Commissioner Kubilius calls for new European defence architecture within NATO  INSIGHT EU MONITORING

Warsaw, 12 October 2026
At the inauguration of the new European Security and Strategy programme at the College of Europe in Natolin, EU Commissioner Andrius Kubilius called for a European Defence Union and Security Council. He outlined a new security architecture within NATO, responding to Russia’s military expansion, shifting US priorities and Ukraine’s strategic role.
Ten key takeaways
- Russia’s military expansion threatens European security. Kubilius warns that Russia is preparing for prolonged confrontation, with military spending projected at €180 billion in 2027, a 33% increase. In purchasing power parity terms, he estimates Russian defence expenditure could match the EU’s combined spending of €500–550 billion. He also warns that Russia could eventually deploy 10 million drones annually.
- NATO 3.0 requires Europeans to assume primary responsibility for conventional defence. As the United States increasingly redirects strategic resources towards the Indo-Pacific in response to China’s growing military and economic power, Europeans must take responsibility for their territorial defence. Kubilius expects the US to retain a secondary conventional role and maintain its nuclear umbrella.
- Europe needs a new security architecture within 10–15 years. Kubilius advocates a fundamental transformation from a predominantly transatlantic defence system towards European collective defence. His proposed Europe 3.0 concept would establish defence as a core dimension of European integration alongside the free movement of people and goods.
- A European Defence Union and Security Council could transform decision-making. Kubilius supports Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal for a European Security Council involving partners such as Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the United Kingdom. He envisages a European Defence Union anchored in Article 42(7) TEU, providing a stronger European pillar within NATO that is separable but not separate from the Alliance.
- China and India could fundamentally reshape the global economic order. Kubilius anticipates that China and India could become the world’s two largest economies by the end of the century, potentially pushing the United States into third place and the EU into fourth. He describes this as a historic reversal of the economic balance between East and West, requiring Europe to adapt its geopolitical strategy.
- A stronger EU-US strategic partnership could preserve Western influence. Kubilius argues that neither Europe nor the United States can independently prevent the relative economic rise of China and India. He proposes a new phase of Westernization, bringing Europe and America into a more integrated strategic community capable of maintaining global economic, technological and geopolitical influence.
- Russia’s long-term transformation is essential for lasting European peace. Kubilius considers Russia’s future the most unpredictable among the major geopolitical powers. Continued authoritarian aggression could lead to economic decline, instability or even state collapse. He argues that sustainable European security ultimately requires Russia to become a peaceful, responsible state, while rejecting an unconditional reset with President Vladimir Putin.
- Ukraine’s military victory and EU integration could encourage political change in Russia. Kubilius identifies three European instruments for influencing Russia’s long-term trajectory: supporting Ukraine’s military success, enabling its economic and social development through EU integration, and establishing a future framework for EU-Russia relations. Renewed economic cooperation with Russia should depend on its abandonment of aggressive policies.
- Poland, Germany and Ukraine could become the backbone of European defence. Kubilius proposes a strategic defence pillar centred on Poland, Germany and Ukraine, complemented by the Nordic and Baltic countries. Within NATO 3.0 and Europe 3.0, this regional configuration would form a central component of Europe’s future collective defence architecture, strengthening the continent’s eastern security capabilities.
- European integration must overcome national fragmentation. Kubilius argues that Europe’s ability to address major geopolitical transformations depends on collective ambition rather than competing national priorities. He calls for an intellectual transformation alongside financial, industrial and institutional reforms, urging a new generation of European leaders to develop the ideas needed for a more sovereign, united and strategically capable European Union.

articles.title: Ceasefire along front lines and lifting of sanctions against russia: WP columnist reveals details of US and European peace plan - Ukrainian news
articles.summary: Ceasefire along front lines and lifting of sanctions against russia: WP columnist reveals details of US and European peace plan  Ukrainian news
articles.full_text:
The United States and European countries are developing a joint peace plan for Ukraine. It calls for a freeze in hostilities along the front lines, a phased lifting of sanctions against russia, large-scale investments in Ukraine’s reconstruction, and security guarantees for the country. Columnist David Ignatius wrote about this in a column for The Washington Post, citing sources. He believes the plan is a “territorial compromise neither side will like,” but that a package of accompanying measures should make it more acceptable to both.
According to Ignatius, the “diplomatic push” occurred last Friday during a six-hour meeting in Florida. The meeting was attended by US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, as well as representatives from Ukraine, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany. One US official explained the logic behind the approach.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the columnist quotes him as saying.
According to Ignatius, a condition for implementing the initiative is the cessation of Ukrainian strikes on russian oil refineries.
What the peace plan offers russia?
Putin is being offered not only to end the war but also to conclude an economic and security agreement with Europe. It must take into account russia’s “security concerns,” although, as the columnist notes, it is not yet clear exactly what that will entail. Another element could be an energy agreement between russia, Ukraine, and Europe. One option is a pipeline to supply russian oil and gas to Europe, with profits shared between Ukraine and russia. The peace agreement should also specify which sanctions against russia will be lifted and when.
What security guarantees will Ukraine receive?
Under the plan, the US and European countries are to pledge a military response to Ukraine in the event of a new russian attack. According to a US official, such commitments would be equivalent to Article 5 of the NATO Charter on collective defense.
Who will finance Ukraine’s reconstruction?
The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock are to establish a special mechanism for post-war reconstruction. The funds are intended to be used for rebuilding destroyed areas, providing compensation to the families of fallen and wounded soldiers, and reviving the economy. US negotiators have already asked the Ukrainian side to provide a detailed cost estimate and guarantees of transparent use of the funds.
What the plan entails regarding territories?
The key and most contentious point is a freeze on hostilities along the current front line. According to the columnist, russia must agree to a ceasefire along the line of contact, while Ukraine must recognize russia’s control over the occupied territories. One of the obstacles remains the uncertainty regarding exactly where this line runs.
The column was published amid a public conflict between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy over a deal to supply diesel fuel. Ignatius notes that more than a year and a half ago, Trump claimed that Zelenskyy “has no cards" to play, yet now he is protesting Ukraine’s devastating strikes on russian oil refineries.
It is worth noting that russia had previously refused to end the war without control over the entire Donbas, while Ukraine ruled out officially recognizing russian control over the occupied territories.

14 October 2026 – CBAM imposes costs on both sides of the Atlantic. The US Trade Representative is collecting evidence until 9 November on the burden for US exporters. In Germany, the announced restructuring of Deutsche Edelstahlwerke shows that it is not imports, but CBAM, energy prices and tariffs that are weighing on demand.
Deutsche Edelstahlwerke: Too Few Tariffs Were Never the Problem
Since 1 July, the Steel Regulation has protected the EU market with a 50 per cent tariff outside the quotas. Three and a half months later, Swiss Steel Group is restructuring Deutsche Edelstahlwerke. Hagen and Krefeld are up for sale, otherwise closure threatens. The Siegen steelworks is pausing production. Around 970 employees work at these sites.
Import Pressure? Not in the Numbers
Swiss Steel cites “increasing import pressure” as one of several burdens. Eurostat data for 2026 do not show it. From January to July, third country imports across all DEW product groups were below the previous year, with forged bars down 34 per cent. Imports of stainless steel bars fell by 42 per cent in July, the first month under the Regulation.
According to the Group, sales at Hagen have more than halved since 2018. Volumes lost after the 2021 floods never returned, and more than 70 per cent of customers come from the automotive industry. EU imports of stainless steel wire rod fell by one third over the same period. The flood did not come from China.
Swiss Steel says it itself: “Trade policy measures can provide short term relief, but they do not change these structural challenges.”
Weak Demand Is Politically Made
DEW’s customers pay European energy prices, CO2 costs and CBAM on imported input materials. Since July, tight quotas have been added, with a 50 per cent tariff on everything above them.
Make automotive manufacturing and mechanical engineering this expensive and falling sales are the result. In our view, this is not market weakness. It is political failure in Brussels and Berlin.
Krefeld as a Signal to Brussels
Krefeld forges tool steel. This product is not covered by the Regulation, and the Commission is assessing by 31 December whether it should be included. Yet in 2025, the EU exported more forged tool steel than it imported. We read the announcement for what it does politically: it creates pressure to include precisely these product groups in the upcoming review.
Our Position
We fundamentally oppose tariffs, regardless of direction. For us, they are a core instrument of socialist and communist economic control: the state decides at the border who may buy what, and at what price. But principle does not mean slogans. As Gerber Group, we submitted a clear, data based position against the Steel Regulation in the review consultation. If there is a Have Your Say procedure, we will do so again.
Anyone now demanding more tariffs is prescribing the next round of higher costs for steel customers and the next demand gap for the mills.
How Burdensome Is CBAM? Washington Wants to Know
The Office of the United States Trade Representative, USTR, wants to know what the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, CBAM, costs American exporters.
Until 9 November 2026, companies can submit comments on regulations.gov under docket number USTR-2026-0661. The USTR is asking about costs, bureaucracy and market access, explicitly including the impact on small and medium sized businesses, disadvantages compared with EU competitors and possible enforcement measures.
Brussels Provides the Evidence
The notice identifies exactly what Stainless Espresso has been criticising for months: default values with a punitive mark up and company data that may only be verified by an EU accredited verifier. Substantial bureaucracy costs, which the Commission recently had to revise upwards by more than 40 per cent. At the same time, the Commission, Council and Parliament want to expand CBAM to more than 450 downstream product groups.
Figures for Washington
We encourage all US companies to participate actively. If you need facts to support your position against CBAM, please contact us. We will provide the figures you need.

PARIS, FRANCE — French HR services group HR Path has bought SnapAI, a Paris start-up focused on AI governance and compliance, as employers prepare for European rules that treat AI in hiring and employee management as high-risk. The deal gives HR Path’s consulting and outsourcing clients in-house help to deploy AI within those rules.
Compliance expertise for HR
The European Union’s AI Act, which is being rolled out in phases through 2028, classifies AI used in recruitment, assessment and employee management as high-risk, Staffing Industry Analysts reported. HR Path said SnapAI’s governance and compliance expertise will help clients deploy AI in a way that is both ambitious and controlled.
Terms were not disclosed, and HR Path declined to comment on the price. SnapAI, co-founded by Ahmed Salama and Pierre Soulier, helps organizations identify and understand their AI use cases, and Soulier is joining HR Path as part of the transaction.
AI across advise, implement and outsource
HR Path operates in 34 countries with nearly 2,900 employees and serves clients through three service lines: advise, implement and outsource. It wants AI to run across all three, from AI strategy work in consulting to integrating AI into HR software and automating selected activities in its outsourcing business.
The group has set up a task force dedicated to AI and recently launched an AI offering that covers maturity assessments, use case selection, process redesign and adoption.
“By combining our AI expertise with HR Path’s in-depth knowledge of HR functions, technological expertise and international presence, we will be able to develop new use cases and support organisations much more broadly in this transformation,” Salama and Soulier said.
The deal will also help HR Path speed up the integration of AI across its offerings and develop new uses for HR functions. Founded in 2001, the group has made technology innovation central to its growth. HR Path says AI should reduce repetitive tasks and free up time for higher-value work.
For companies that outsource HR, the deal signals that providers will be expected to show AI compliance, not just AI features. Buyers of HR outsourcing and payroll outsourcing services in Europe should ask how partners classify and document the AI they use in hiring and employee management. Companies comparing AI-focused partners can start with the top AI outsourcing companies.

Ukrainians strike refineries again — without Starlink (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,694)  EUobserverRussia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume  BBCRussia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses  The GuardianZelenskyy defies Trump as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries  Financial TimesUkraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskiy says 'we're done' with T...
articles.full_text:
Every day, the Ukraine Battlefield update newsletter offers a clear look at how the war is unfolding on the ground. Subscribe for free here to get the full text delivered to your inbox.
- Zelensky has lost patience; the US is acting as Putin’s ally.
- How Ukrainians attacked Russian targets without Starlink.
- If Musk did not switch off Starlink, who did? The main suspects.
- Ukrainian attacks on data centres hit Russia where it hurts.
- Why this type of attack will continue to escalate and not only in this war.
- Videos of the day: a hero robot returns without a wheel; attacks on ammunition depots.
Zelensky has lost patience; the US is Putin’s ally. Despite problems with Starlink, which Kyiv said cut connections with attack drones when they exceeded a certain speed, major Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory continued in recent hours. Long-range strikes over Russia are carried out by drones without Starlink.
These included an attack on the military airfield in Borisoglebsk, more than 300 km from the border, as well as on a refinery in Ryazan, which the local governor confirmed. The Ryazan refinery belongs to Rosneft and is one of the largest, with a capacity of around 17 million tonnes of oil a year.
This came after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times that he had had enough after Russian attacks during the so-called energy truce, and announced that refineries would once again become Ukrainian targets.
It was precisely a limitation of such Ukrainian strikes that US president Donald Trump had demanded, after last week concluding a controversial agreement with Moscow to buy Russian oil without asking for anything in return from the Russian side.
This was followed by steps that raised serious suspicions that Trump had begun acting in favour of Putin’s war against Ukraine.
The US threatened Ukraine with restricting supplies of weapons or critically important intelligence and, ultimately, as we examined on Wednesday in the Ukraine Battlefield update, Ukrainian soldiers began experiencing a serious problem with the full internet connection provided by the military version of Starlink, which Musk’s SpaceX developed for the Pentagon.
This is crucial to the Ukrainian army not only for attacks on Russian logistics at the front, but also in defending against more dangerous Russian jet-powered drones, which have terrorised Ukrainian cities in recent months.
Russia's pro-Kremlin scene naturally noticed this as well. The Z-blogger Rybar called for the use of an “opportunity” in which Russian forces could inflict maximum damage on Ukrainian infrastructure.
“I think the crisis is entirely clear and understandable. The crisis lies in Trump's position, which is trying to help Russia in every possible way,” expert Volodymyr Ohryzko commented on the situation.
We write below about what the company's owner, Elon Musk, has said about these developments.
How Ukrainians attacked without Starlink. In the first of the Ukrainian attacks mentioned above, on the airfield in Borisoglebsk, Ukrainian Neptune missiles were used, according to the Ukrainian navy. Ukrainians said they destroyed as many as six Su-34M aircraft. They have their own navigation systems and do not need SpaceX services.
The attack on the refinery in Ryazan involved drones that are likewise not connected to Starlink, as SpaceX has geographically restricted Ukraine's access to both Starlink and Starshield services.
“The Ukrainian armed forces therefore rely on alternative means of communication and point-to-point navigation to strike targets in Russia. The speed restrictions under the Starshield service are unrelated to this and will not prevent the Ukrainian armed forces from attacking Russian oil refineries, data centres and other stationary targets in Russia,” the Institute for the Study of War said.
However, Ukrainians felt the problems mainly at the home front.
An unnamed Ukrainian officer compared it to nuclear strikes in comments to Politico. “All operations have been suspended. It will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced soldier commanding a medium-range unmanned aircraft unit in south-eastern Ukraine told the Brussels-based website.
They use Hornet drones to attack targets at distances of up to 150 km.
Ukrainian soldiers contacted by Politico said the restrictions had halted some medium-range drone attacks over Ukraine, disrupting strikes on Russian logistics and reducing support for Ukrainian units at the front.
The scale of the disruption is unclear, however, and it is not known whether the restriction remains in place.
If Musk did not switch off Starlink, who did? The main suspects. Several Ukrainian soldiers reported on Wednesday that they had had to suspend their operations because of restrictions on satellite connections with drones that exceeded 160 km/h.
According to former minister Mykhailo Fedorov, this capability was later restored. NV sources, by contrast, said the speed limit remained in place on Wednesday evening. The following day, operation of the system was fully restored, according to Ukraine's defence ministry, while the circumstances of the outage are being investigated.
Importantly, Zelensky said it was not a technical problem but an apparent deliberate act. It is not yet certain who was behind it, although the main suspect is clear.
Musk claims that, because the military version of the Starshield satellite internet connection is military in nature, it is controlled by the US government, which also owns it.
“Any decisions on speed or usage restrictions are made by the US military and, ultimately, the US president (POTUS),” the world's richest man wrote on his social network X. However, the White House, according to Axios sources, claims it had nothing to do with the restriction and wants Musk's company to investigate the circumstances.
Republican senator Tom Tillis is also calling for this in Congress. “I do not expect defence secretary Hegseth to ensure transparency, and therefore we will ask the defence department's inspector general to launch an investigation and report to Congress and the American people,” he wrote on X.
Starshield differs from the regular network in its greater resistance to jamming and its specialisation for military use.
Oleksandr “Serg Marco” Karpiuk, a well-known Ukrainian specialist in military aerial reconnaissance, wrote on Facebook that standard Starlink terminals currently have a preset speed limit of 22 m/s.
“To be able to fly at speeds above 22 m/s, Ukraine signed contracts for the Starshield system, which is managed by the Pentagon. This is a military system using Starlink terminals that offer greater functionality, although these accounts are substantially more expensive,” he explained. According to him, the Pentagon did two things within a single day: it restricted intelligence-sharing and changed the parameters of Starshield accounts.
“It was a decision by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, evidently on Trump's orders,” Karpiuk believes, as quoted by Illia Ponomarenko in a post.
Pro-Kremlin propaganda has welcomed the latest developments.
The Russian daily Kommersant quoted a Musk post in which he wrote that it was “time for Zelensky to leave”. His words followed Trump once again pushing Ukraine to hold elections in which it would choose a new president.
Zelensky responded that they would be happy to organise elections if Russia observed a 60-day ceasefire.
Experts agree that it is unrealistic to organise a proper vote under the wartime conditions Ukraine faces.
Ukrainian attacks on data centres hit Russia where it hurts. Although it has not yet been confirmed that pro-Kremlin bots became less active after Ukrainian drones struck Russian servers, ordinary Russians felt the impact. Russia started such attacks in September, amid escalating air raids on Kyiv.
As many as around 100,000 households lost internet access at the time. Now, this tactic has been turned against Moscow.
Researchers studying Russian trolling did not observe any real decline in the activity of pro-Putin bots either, according to a BBC analysis. Far more interesting, however, are the real-world consequences of Ukrainian attacks on the data centres of Yandex, Russia's Google, which have manifested themselves in a range of ways.
According to Politico sources, Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that it takes two to play this game. According to the Financial Times, they have already managed to seriously damage three of Yandex's six data centres: in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir.
The consequences of these attacks subsequently showed how vulnerable Russia's centralised internet ecosystem is.
“Russia has become a victim of its own policies, which has led to the worst possible scenario,” Alena Epifanova, an expert at the German Council on Foreign Relations, told the FT.
The impact of the Ukrainian attack has affected the daily lives of Russians. Here overview of services that were affected to a greater or lesser extent, according to the British daily:
- problems accessing Yandex email;
- Yandex Taxi was taken offline;
- several websites — including a dating app and the Russian equivalent of McDonald's — were inaccessible;
- saved files and documents could not be opened;
- bus timetables disappeared in some cities;
- residents of some Moscow apartment buildings could not get through electric gates;
- banking services were not fully operational.
All the affected data centres also have supercomputers used to train AI, which is playing an increasingly important role on the battlefield.
For example, one of Yandex's three supercomputers — Chervonenkis — in Sasovo had long ranked among the world's 100 most powerful supercomputers, and only in 2026 fell to 101st place, according to the BBC.
However, it has not been confirmed that Ukrainian attacks damaged any of them. According to the Russians, an attack on a similar Sberbank facility did not cause significant damage.

articles.summary: Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

EU leaders are meeting in Brussels for a packed two-day summit. Energy prices, trade with China and the budget dominated Thursday's session.
Following today's inconclusive summit, António Costa, the president of the European Council, has taken charge of the EU budget negotiations.
Costa intends to reflect on the feedback provided by member states, which are still attached to their red lines and maximalist positions, and propose a new compromise text in the coming weeks.
The compromise will seek to explore a different logic than the one proposed by Ireland, which alarmed Brussels by cutting heavily on the emergency funds of the so-called EU Facility. Officials say the lessons from the past years (COVID, Ukraine, energy crisis, climate change) justify leaving a considerable amount of funds unallocated.
Another key priority for Costa is the New Own Resources, the EU-wide taxes that are meant to bring additional revenue into the common pot.
A special summit dedicated to the budget will be held on 26 November. Costa's compromise should be proposed before then.

The press conference of the summit's first day has been cancelled after the debate on the next EU budget ran for too long. In parallel, a battle over the Emissions Trading System kept aides occupied.
Leaders have now moved to dinner, dedicated to enlargement and internal reforms.
Italy and Sweden clash over energy rules with conclusions at risk
Energy has emerged as the most contentious issue at the summit so far.
After three hours of debate, EU leaders turned to discussions on the bloc’s budget. However, diplomats were still negotiating the conclusions, with Italy and Sweden on opposing sides, according to two diplomats.
Rome is backing the four Visegrad countries — Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland — in calling for the next Emissions Trading System (ETS2) to be postponed until 2030.
They argue that the conditions for introducing the system in 2028 have changed because of the war in the Middle East.
According to a third diplomat, the summit risks ending without endorsed conclusions on the 27 on one of the most politically sensitive issues.
Zelenskyy and Tusk meet
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a bilateral meeting with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on the sidelines of the EU summit.
"We are not just neighbours. We are friends who can count on each other in difficult times. And no one will ever change that," Tusk said.
Relations between the two countries took a tumble earlier this year after Zelenskyy renamed a military unit in homage to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). The UPA is admired in Ukraine for its resistance against the Soviet Union and the pursuit of an independent state. But in Poland, the UPA is held responsible for the massacres of Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia, which Warsaw considers genocide.
Tusk, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, has striven to overcome the rivalry to focus on the common security threat: Russia.
"I thanked Donald for his clear and principled position on sanctions: there must be no steps that help Russia continue this war," Zelenskyy said.

EU budget talks lasting longer than expected
The discussions on the EU budget are lasting longer than originally expected and could take an additional two hours. The press conference tentatively scheduled for 19.30 CET has been delayed but should take place before leaders have dinner.
Leaders will close the day with a strategic debate on enlargement.

Russia launched around 1,000 drones against Ukraine since midnight on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, accusing Moscow of brazenly flouting Donald Trump's calls to reduce attacks.
"Unfortunately, Russia responded to yet another attempt by the American President to reduce the intensity of strikes with new waves of attacks on our energy, residential buildings, and other infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

The reported shortage comes amid mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington over US President Donald Trump's recent deal to import Russian diesel and pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes against Russia's oil infrastructure.

articles.summary: NATO official praises Türkiye’s defence industry, citing long-running industrial revolution  AzerNews
articles.full_text:
By News Centre
NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska has praised the level achieved by Türkiye’s defence industry, emphasizing that the country has been experiencing what amounts to a de facto industrial revolution in the sector for a long time and has developed outstanding examples of defence innovation.
Shekerinska spoke alongside Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to NATO, Ambassador Basat Öztürk, during a session titled “NATO and Europe: Security Architecture Following the Ankara Summit” at the Türkiye-EU Business Summit in Brussels. The event was organized in cooperation with the Foreign Economic Relations Board of Türkiye (DEİK) and the European Business Summit (EBS).
Shekerinska said discussions at the NATO Summit held in Ankara on July 7–8 focused on translating the commitments on defence spending made at the Hague Summit into concrete capabilities. She noted that European allies and Canada were assuming greater responsibility for the Alliance’s security.
European allies and Canada allocated more than an additional $250 billion to defence in 2025 and 2026, Shekerinska said, describing the increase as “a rational response to a security environment that has changed significantly in recent years.”
She noted that burden-sharing had been a subject of discussion within NATO since the Alliance’s establishment. At the Ankara Summit, however, progress was made in increasing defence spending, expanding procurement contracts and strengthening cooperation in the defence sector. Shekerinska said contracts worth approximately $50 billion had been announced and signed.
She emphasized that the primary objective was to go beyond increasing expenditure and ensure that the additional resources translated into the capabilities NATO needed.
One of the key messages emerging from the Ankara Summit, Shekerinska said, was the vision of “a stronger Europe within a stronger Alliance.” She added that European allies and Canada would assume greater responsibility, particularly in the area of conventional deterrence.
Shekerinska also warned that hybrid threats and attacks could be as dangerous as other forms of aggression, highlighting what she described as Russia’s increasingly reckless and dangerous actions.
According to Shekerinska, Russia has failed to achieve a significant advantage on the battlefield in recent months and has been losing more than 40,000 troops every month. Despite these losses, she said, Moscow has continued to pursue hybrid activities aimed at undermining allied support for Ukraine. These activities include attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine, airspace violations, sabotage, arson and threats of assassination.
“That is why we say that NATO will continue to remain calm, because we know that we are militarily superior and stronger. We will continue on our path. This means sustaining our investments and preserving the technological superiority and advantage we possess,” Shekerinska said.
She stressed the importance of maintaining support for Ukraine, arguing that the Alliance must demonstrate that Russia cannot achieve a strategic victory by weakening that assistance.
The war in Ukraine has demonstrated the importance of technology in defence and accelerated innovation processes, Shekerinska said, adding that data-driven defence solutions would play an increasingly decisive role in the future.
“That is why we have spoken so much about the defence industry. We also have excellent examples in the Turkish defence industry. This is because we have been witnessing what is effectively an industrial revolution here, and this has been happening for a long time, not just over the past few years,” she said.
Shekerinska highlighted the importance of artificial intelligence-based solutions and systems designed to counter unmanned aerial vehicles. She also underlined the need for companies to cooperate in order to preserve innovation across the defence industry.
In this context, she said NATO supported reducing barriers to trade and cooperation as much as possible. The Alliance also favoured making greater use of the capabilities of defence industries on both sides of the Atlantic, as well as those of allied countries that are not members of the European Union.
Shekerinska noted that NATO also maintained close cooperation with countries in the Asia-Pacific region. However, she said overall production capacity had yet to reach the level required to meet the Alliance’s objectives.
In addition to the contracts signed at the Ankara Summit, Shekerinska said, production capacity had increased by $38 billion. She stressed that industrial capacity could provide a strategic advantage during prolonged conflicts, when the ability to sustain the production and supply of military equipment becomes particularly important.
Shekerinska also addressed developments in the Black Sea region, reporting that NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had held talks with Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova earlier that morning. She said allied countries were providing additional assistance to facilitate the progress of the investigation.
Shekerinska said Ukraine was waging a defensive war and that the current situation was the consequence of Russia’s decision to attack the country.
She concluded by noting that NATO’s focus extended beyond the Black Sea to encompass its entire eastern flank, stretching from the Arctic to the Black Sea. Work to strengthen security across this area was continuing, she added.

The European Union is preparing to lift trade restrictions on an unnamed Chinese company accused of helping Russia’s war against Ukraine as part of a deal with Beijing aimed at protecting a key supplier to ASML Holding NV, Bloomberg reported on October 14.
According to Bloomberg, the proposed arrangement would see China remove restrictions on Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, a small German company that supplies components within ASML’s semiconductor production chain.
In return, the EU would lift restrictions imposed on the unnamed Chinese company under its 21st sanctions package against Russia. That package targeted several Chinese firms accused of supplying Moscow with key components that could be used in weapons production.
China sanctioned Sindlhauser and 13 other European companies in July in retaliation for the EU measures, Bloomberg reported. Sindlhauser specializes in high-precision manufacturing and advanced coatings for the semiconductor industry and other sectors.
Brussels and Beijing have also agreed to exchange more information and provide warning of future export restrictions, according to people familiar with the talks.
Bloomberg noted that removing Sindlhauser and the Chinese company from their respective restrictions could establish a model for resolving similar sanctions disputes in the future.
The talks come as Europe tries to protect strategic semiconductor supply chains while maintaining pressure on companies accused of supporting Russia’s military-industrial base. ASML, headquartered in the Netherlands, is one of the world’s most important manufacturers of advanced chipmaking equipment.
Earlier this month, an investigation traced Chinese-made electronics, batteries, radio equipment, and other components to a Russian company linked to the Kurier combat robot. articles.title: Farmers told to secure 75% of fertiliser before UK carbon tax hits imports in January 2027 - Conservative Post
articles.summary: Farmers told to secure 75% of fertiliser before UK carbon tax hits imports in January 2027  Conservative Post
articles.full_text:
Farmers are being advised to have 75% of their fertiliser requirements ordered for delivery before the end of the year, as buying picks up ahead of the introduction of the UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
Frontier Agriculture said although fertiliser purchases have increased over the past three to four weeks, the market remains behind where it would normally be at this stage of the season. The recent increase has been driven primarily by crops going into the ground and beginning to establish, but CBAM is also influencing purchasing decisions alongside concerns over availability, logistics and wider upward price pressure.
The advice was set out in a report published by Farmers Guide on 7 October 2026.
Frontier has advised growers who have yet to secure their 2027 fertiliser requirements to continue with a “little-and-often” purchasing strategy.
It said: “At this stage we would advise growers to now have 75% of their requirements ordered for delivery before the end of the year – if it isn’t already on farm.
“This gives room for further purchases to take account of changes to cropping areas, future market movements and when we eventually understand the true cost impact of CBAM in year one.”
CBAM takes effect from 1 January 2027 and places a carbon cost on the emissions embodied in certain imported goods, including fertiliser. In HMRC’s official policy paper, the mechanism is described as a new tax ensuring that highly traded, carbon intensive imports face a carbon price comparable to that paid by manufacturers producing the same goods in the UK under the UK Emissions Trading Scheme.
The market remains behind
While demand on farm is now broadly in line with what would normally be expected at this point in the season, Frontier said a significant shortfall earlier in the year means cumulative demand remains below typical levels. The industry is still carrying what Frontier called a “sizeable seasonal deficit” and remains under pressure to organise stocks ahead of spring demand.
Nitrogen-based solid products, particularly ammonium nitrate (AN) and urea, alongside liquid UAN, are currently seeing the greatest demand. Demand for products containing sulphur is also increasing, with Frontier expecting further buying due to the larger oilseed rape area.
Frontier said the immediate concern is less about overall product supply and more about the industry’s ability to move fertiliser onto farms when it is needed. With around 55 delivery days remaining this year, there is a limited window to catch up before the traditionally busy spring delivery period.
A tax made in Westminster
CBAM is a British tax, charged to the importer when the product enters the UK rather than when it is delivered to farm. Its path into law is a matter of record.
The policy was set out by the Conservative government in a consultation launched in March 2023, when Jeremy Hunt was chancellor, and the Treasury confirmed in its December 2023 consultation response that the UK would introduce a CBAM. A further consultation on the design ran from March to June 2024, and the October 2024 response fixed key decisions on scope.
The Labour government then confirmed the start date at the Autumn Budget on 30 October 2024, when Rachel Reeves was chancellor, with the measure scored in the budget documents. Provision for HMRC to prepare the tax was included in the Finance Act 2025, and the substantive legislation was enacted in Part 5 of the Finance Act 2026, sections 142 to 158 of which establish the CBAM, with section 158 providing that the tax has effect in relation to goods imported into the United Kingdom on or after 1 January 2027. Both Acts were passed under the current Labour administration. Further design decisions were confirmed at Budget 2025, including the exclusion of indirect emissions at implementation.
The tax applies to imported goods from the aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel sectors. Businesses importing £50,000 or more of these goods over a 12-month period must register with HMRC. The tax applies to relevant imports from 1 January 2027, and government guidance states that registration for CBAM will open by 1 January 2028. Importers who become liable before registration opens must keep records of the CBAM goods they have imported so they can register when the service is available. The Exchequer impact is scored at £140 million for 2027 to 2028, rising to £180 million the following year, figures certified by the Office for Budget Responsibility.
Britain’s fertiliser industry relies on imported ammonia
The tax lands on a fertiliser market that no longer has a domestic nitrogen base. CF Fertilisers UK announced in July 2023 that it would permanently close its ammonia plant at Billingham, the largest in the country, after the closure of the Ince plant in 2022. The company said it would continue producing ammonium nitrate at Billingham using imported ammonia.
Frontier has therefore warned that costs associated with CBAM will ultimately be felt across imported nitrogen fertiliser. The eventual CBAM charge will be determined by three factors: the carbon cost, based on the UK Emissions Trading Scheme; the embedded emissions associated with the product; and a free allowance adjustment.
Frontier said some of the figures needed to make that calculation remain unknown, making it impossible to currently calculate the precise cost of CBAM on a product.
It said: “CBAM will increase the cost of every fertiliser which contains nitrogen that is used in the UK arriving after 1st January 2027.
“The challenge currently is that the industry is awaiting further clarity from the government in order to understand how much that cost will be, so as it stands, the full implications remain unknown.”
The industry has already pushed back
The pressure on the Treasury is not new. In April 2026 the NFU formally called for a delay to CBAM, having previously warned it would push up the cost of fertiliser for farmers, particularly in the arable sector. NFU Scotland raised the same concerns in August 2026, warning the mechanism could increase fertiliser costs and squeeze farm margins further.
In May 2026, The Guardian reported that ministers had held talks over suspending the carbon tax on fertiliser to curb food inflation, with fertiliser prices at the time running around £618 a tonne according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.
CBAM is charged at the border, so fertiliser delivered after 1 January will not necessarily be subject to the charge if it has already entered the country. Frontier has previously advised that purchasing decisions should not be based solely on CBAM, but has said the mechanism needs to be considered as part of growers’ wider plans. The company has also called for joined-up government action on fertiliser policy.
Frontier’s head of crop nutrition, Ed Downing, said: “Fundamentally, if buying fertiliser now is the right decision based on the market, then it will also avoid any CBAM cost, helping to further reduce some risk in the short term. But it really comes down to the individual farm.”
Great British PAC reaction
Claire Bullivant, Chief Executive of the Great British PAC, said:
“What on earth is this Labour Government playing at? British farmers are already being hammered by rising costs, squeezed margins and relentless uncertainty, and now Labour is pressing ahead with another tax that threatens to make producing British food even more expensive.
“Think about the sheer madness of this. We have lost our domestic ammonia production, we depend on imports, and now the Government wants to slap a carbon charge on the fertiliser our farmers need to grow the food that feeds our nation. Worse still, with just weeks to go, the industry cannot even tell farmers how much it is going to cost them. What sort of way is that to run a country?
“Farmers cannot plant uncertainty, harvest government promises or pay their bills with Net Zero slogans. They need affordable fertiliser, fair conditions and a government that understands the difference between protecting the environment and punishing the people who produce our food.
“And who does Labour think will ultimately pay when the cost of growing food rises? British families, of course. The very people already struggling with the cost of living.
“You cannot tax British farming into prosperity, and you cannot build food security by making it more expensive to grow food in Britain.
“Food security is national security. Our farmers are not the enemy. They are the backbone of this country, and it is about time Westminster started treating them that way.”
And Richard Thomson, former Royal Marine and National Director of Great British PAC added:
„Britain’s farmers have already been hammered by soaring costs, punishing taxes and endless regulation. Now they are being told to stockpile fertiliser before Rachel Reeves’s carbon border tax takes effect.
This is Net Zero ideology colliding with economic reality.
Fertiliser is not a luxury. It is essential to growing food. Make it more expensive and farmers pay more, British agriculture becomes less competitive, and families face higher prices at the checkout.
A government that destroys its own agriculture in pursuit of arbitrary carbon targets is not protecting the environment. It is undermining our industry, our food security and our national independence.“

articles.title: John Healey plots £1billion VAT crackdown on major online marketplaces to fund high street tax cut - GB News
articles.summary: John Healey plots £1billion VAT crackdown on major online marketplaces to fund high street tax cut  GB NewsJohn Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget  The GuardianUK finance minister Healey to target online marketplaces in tax crackdown, The Times reports  ReutersJohn Healey plans £1bn Budget crackdown on online retailers  The TelegraphChancellor in online marketplace tax crackdown as he plots ‘white van man’ Budget &nb...
articles.full_text:
Chancellor John Healey is preparing a £1billion tax raid on major online marketplaces in his maiden Budget.
The crackdown will force the e-commerce platforms to collect VAT directly from retailers selling goods on their sites for the first time.
Online marketplaces would be responsible for collecting VAT when customers buy from business sellers whose annual turnover exceeds £90,000, under the plans reported by The Times.
The proposal aims to tackle a loophole used mainly by overseas sellers to avoid paying VAT, taking advantage of weak enforcement.
Mr Healey expects the change to raise up to £1billion, which would fund cuts to business rates for high street shops.
Concerns about tax avoidance by overseas retailers have grown in recent years, particularly over Chinese sellers setting up sham UK companies.
Chinese nationals have set up tens of thousands of shell companies in the UK, using their VAT registration numbers to appear as British sellers on online marketplaces. The accounts are then abandoned before tax demands arrive.
MPs on the Public Accounts Committee have accused HMRC of failing to take the issue seriously enough. They warned that overseas sellers exploiting gaps in enforcement were undercutting British businesses.
In 2025, the committee said the estimated £5.5billion lost each year through these practices could be just the "tip of the iceberg".
There is no suggestion that the online marketplaces themselves have acted improperly.
During the Makerfield by-election, Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to raise the business rates threshold so that 140,000 small high street shops would no longer have to pay the tax at all.
The commitment was estimated to cost around £880million.
Mr Burnham said at the time that he wanted to support family-owned businesses, which he described as the "heart and soul of this country", and give them "the chance to thrive".
A Treasury source explained that Mr Healey's goal was to "protect local family businesses and the high streets we love".
Mr Burnham had previously suggested funding the business rates relief by imposing a new tax on out-of-town warehouses, but ministers have now abandoned that idea following fierce opposition from retail leaders.
John Lewis executive chairman Jason Tarry said last week that a warehouse levy would "reveal a fundamental misunderstanding of how modern high streets work".
Industry figures warned that taxing warehouses would inevitably drive up costs for retailers and ultimately lead to higher prices for consumers.
The decision to target online sellers instead is likely to sit more comfortably with the retail sector, which has long argued that bricks-and-mortar shops face an unfair tax burden compared with their digital rivals.
An Amazon spokesman said: "Closing this loophole will raise significant revenue for the exchequer and simplify compliance for both HMRC and legitimate sellers."
Dan Neidle, founder of Tax Policy Associates, cautioned that the £90,000 threshold leaves room for continued abuse.
He said: "This is a step in the right direction but the Treasury needs to go further and make online marketplaces responsible for collecting every penny of VAT on the sales made on their platform."
He warned: "Unless that happens these Chinese sham companies will find just another way around the rules."The Budget is due on October 28, with Mr Healey facing a challenging fiscal backdrop. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said on Monday that the Chancellor confronts a £35billion bill to maintain current spending commitments and increase defence funding to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030.
The IMF has urged Mr Healey not to pursue unfunded giveaways, while he has already ruled out raising capital gains tax to match income tax rates.

articles.title: TRST01 Announces Full EUDR Readiness For Indian Coffee, Rubber And Soy Exporters As 30 December Deadline Nears - Outlook Business
articles.summary: TRST01 Announces Full EUDR Readiness For Indian Coffee, Rubber And Soy Exporters As 30 December Deadline Nears  Outlook Business
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Delhi, India: TRST01, the supply chain traceability and Digital Public Infrastructure company, today announced that its TRST01Chain platform and TRST01 EUDR Hub are fully ready to support Indian exporters of coffee, natural rubber and soy in meeting the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which applies to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026.
After two postponements, the EUDR application date is now fixed in law through Regulation (EU) 2025/2650, and the European Commission has signalled that no further delay is planned. Micro and small operators follow on 30 June 2027. With only weeks remaining, TRST01 is urging India's export ecosystem to move from preparation to proof.
Europe's compliance machinery is switched on
The EU has spent 2026 getting its systems ready. The EUDR Information System, through which every Due Diligence Statement must be filed, reopened at the end of June 2026 after a rebuild. In July, the European Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1565 setting the system's technical rules, along with a delegated act that updates the list of covered products. One provision, on how statements are routed to national enforcement authorities, takes effect on 15 October 2026. European buyers are already asking Indian suppliers for plot-level data, not promises.
"Low risk" is not "no work"
India has been benchmarked as a low-risk country under the EU's country classification, which means simplified due diligence for buyers of Indian goods. It is not an exemption. Every consignment still needs geolocation of the land where the commodity was grown, proof that the land was not deforested after 31 December 2020, and evidence that production followed local law.
This is where India is exposed. Indian coffee comes from thousands of small growers in Coorg, Chikkamagaluru and Wayanad, and natural rubber from smallholdings across Kerala, Tamil Nadu and the North-East. Supply chains are fragmented, plot boundaries are rarely mapped as polygons, and supplier records are often on paper. If Indian suppliers cannot deliver clean, verifiable data, EU buyers will shift orders to origins that can, and market share lost in 2027 will not be easy to win back.
Ready across India's key EUDR commodities
Rubber: BSNR puts certified, traceable rubber on the map
India is the world's fifth-largest producer and second-largest consumer of natural rubber, and the Rubber Board of India has moved early. TRST01 powers BSNR, the Board's farm-to-shipment traceability framework, which issues a certificate verifying where the rubber was grown and confirming it meets EUDR requirements. Every transaction is captured in a verifiable, tamper-proof trail, and certification comes at zero cost to farmers and growers, a first for the Board. For European tyre makers and other buyers, Indian natural rubber becomes a ready answer rather than a compliance question.
Coffee: Europe's favourite Indian brew goes digital
India's coffee exports reached a record USD 2.13 billion in FY 2025–26, up about 17% in value, on volumes of roughly 407,000 tonnes. Around 70% of India's coffee is exported, and Europe is the anchor market: Italy, Germany and Belgium lead the buyers, and industry estimates put the EU's share of exports at about 60%. Most Indian coffee is shade-grown under forest-like canopy, which experts say places India better than Brazil or Vietnam to prove "deforestation-free". The Coffee Board is preparing too, with awareness and capacity-building programmes to register growers on its mobile app and digital traceability platform.
20 Indian coffee exporters are already exporting using TRST01Chain, with plot-level geolocation, deforestation checks and lot-by-lot traceability in place for their European buyers. The pressure will only grow: soluble (instant) coffee comes under the EUDR from 30 December 2027. Exporters who build traceability for green coffee now will be ready for instant coffee a year later; those who wait will face two deadlines back to back.
Soy: India's non-GMO advantage
India does not permit commercial cultivation of GM food crops, so its soybean is largely non-GMO, unlike Brazil, the United States and Argentina, where GM varieties dominate. India produced about 11.3 million tonnes of soybean in 2023–24, and soymeal exports are forecast to grow around 13%, with Europe's preference for traceable non-GMO meal the key driver. Under the EUDR, that advantage doubles: Indian soy can offer European feed and food buyers both non-GMO and deforestation-free assurance in a single shipment. In partnership with the Soybean Processors Association of India (SOPA), TRST01 gives member exporters plot-level geo-mapping and EUDR-ready traceability.
TRST01 has built more than 100 EUDR traceability platforms for rubber, coffee and soy across India and seven other countries, and holds reference letters from the Rubber Board of India and the Open AgriTrace Stack (OATS) initiative.
Two products, one compliance chain
TRST01Chain maps farms using TRST01's own drones and other mapping methods, runs proprietary deforestation analysis against the EUDR cut-off date of 31 December 2020, and traces every lot from plot to processor to port on a native AI platform. It is used by more than 200 clients across Southeast Asia, Africa and India.
TRST01 EUDR Hub (eudrhub.cloud), launched in open beta in September 2026, gives operators, suppliers and downstream buyers connected workspaces, so field data flows straight into the due diligence package a European buyer needs to file. Thirteen step-by-step tutorial videos on the TRST01 YouTube channel guide each user type, and operators can begin with a 30-day free trial.
Leadership comment
"India has done the hard part. Our farmers grow world-class coffee and rubber without clearing forests," said Prabir Mishra, Founder and CEO of TRST01. "What we have not yet done, at scale, is prove it in the language Europe now demands. That proof cannot wait for the last week of December. Every exporter, every commodity board and every ministry should treat the weeks ahead as a national sprint. The infrastructure is ready. What we need now is the will to use it."
Call to action
TRST01 is urging India's export ecosystem to act on three fronts before the deadline:
- Exporters should map their supplying plots now, run deforestation checks, and complete a dry run of a full Due Diligence Statement with at least one EU buyer before December.
- Commodity Boards should adopt interoperable, government-owned traceability rails so that small growers are not left behind.
- Ministries should back public-private models in which the government retains ownership and governance of the data, while exporters share the cost through modest per-shipment fees.
India's farmers have earned their place in Europe's market. In the weeks that remain, the country must make sure that place is not lost for want of a map, a file and a digital signature.
Exporters can start a free 30-day trial at eudrhub.cloud or learn more at trst01.com.
About TRST01
TRST01 (TrayamBhu Tech Solutions Private Limited) is a supply chain traceability and Digital Public Infrastructure company with operations across nine countries. Its three flagship platforms are TRST01Chain for supply chain traceability, Footprint for ESG, and Veritas for climate trust and verification. TRST01 combines its own drone mapping, native AI and proprietary deforestation analysis to give complete supply chain visibility, and serves more than 200 clients across Southeast Asia, Africa and India in commodities including rubber, coffee and soy. The company works closely with government bodies, commodity boards and multilateral institutions including the World Bank.
