articles.title: French Student Revolt vs. NATO Spending Push - Orinoco Tribune
articles.summary: French Student Revolt vs. NATO Spending Push  Orinoco Tribune
articles.full_text:
By Medea Benjamin – Oct 12, 2026
An entire generation is being asked to accept austerity while Europe embarks on one of its largest military buildups since the Cold War, writes Medea Benjamin.
For the third week in a row, high school students across France have taken to the streets demanding more investment in their education. They want more teachers, smaller classes, decent school buildings and a public education system that works for poor and working-class students.
But their struggle comes at a moment when France faces mounting pressure to cut public spending while dramatically increasing its military budget. The question at the heart of this uprising goes far beyond education: Will France invest in its young people — or in missiles, weapons, and war? Books or bombs?
What began in the Paris suburbs has spread to more than a thousand schools. On Oct. 6, more than 250,000 people reportedly took to the streets in demonstrations supporting the students.
The government’s response has only deepened the anger. Instead of addressing students’ demands, authorities have unleashed riot police, tear gas, grenades and mass arrests. More than 6,500 people have reportedly been arrested since the protests began, most of them minors. Some young protesters have suffered horrific injuries, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after a police grenade exploded. Amnesty International has condemned what it calls the “disproportionate” use of force against young people peacefully demanding their right to education.
The contrast is striking: Students are asking for teachers and decent schools, while the government deploys riot police against them — and finds billions more for its military.
The student movement is unfolding just as NATO is pressuring European governments to massively increase military spending. Under intense pressure from Washington, NATO leaders agreed in 2025 to a staggering new target: 5 percent of each member country’s GDP by 2035. At least 3.5 percent is supposed to go directly to military expenditures, with another 1.5 percent devoted to military-related infrastructure, cybersecurity, and “resilience.”
This represents an enormous shift from NATO’s previous 2 percent target, which many members already struggled to meet. For countries facing growing deficits, heavy debt and deteriorating public services, such an increase comes at a steep price.
France provides a glaring example. The country has nearly $4 trillion in public debt — roughly 119 percent of GDP, one of the highest levels in Europe. To tackle its deficit, the government has proposed approximately $48 billion in spending cuts and tax increases, putting already strained public services under even greater pressure.
Yet even as the government demands belt-tightening, its proposed 2027 budget increases military spending by approximately $7.2 billion in a single year, compared with just $1.2 billion more for education. The education budget would also eliminate 1,588 permanent teaching positions.
Money for Books, Not Bombs
Imagine being a 16-year-old sitting in an overcrowded classroom, with a leaking ceiling and no regular teacher, hearing that your government cannot afford better schools — but can somehow find billions more for weapons.
France’s own fiscal watchdog has pointed out that increases in central government spending are being driven largely by rising interest payments, contributions to the European Union and increased military expenditures.
NATO officials insist that this massive military buildup is necessary to protect Europe from Russia and other threats. But the notion that Russia is poised to invade France is absurd and the push for ever-greater military spending raises a fundamental question: What kind of security is the French government actually providing if their schools, hospitals and other public services are left to deteriorate?
France is not alone. Students and teachers in Belgium, Spain and Portugal have also taken to the streets over education funding and working conditions, reflecting growing frustration across Europe with governments that claim there is not enough money for basic public services.
An entire generation is being asked to accept austerity while Europe embarks on one of its largest military buildups since the Cold War. Political leaders may insist that education and military spending are separate issues. But they compete for the same limited public resources.
And some French students are already making that connection themselves. Protest signs have declared, “Money for schools, not war” and “Fund high schools, not genocide,” linking their immediate demands to the broader question of what — and whom — the government chooses to fund.
These young people are challenging the very definition of security. NATO measures security in tanks, missiles, drones and ammunition. The students are demanding another kind of security: decent schools, equal opportunity and a society that invests in their future instead of sacrificing it to an endless arms buildup.
Their demands should resonate throughout the NATO alliance, including in the United States, where public services are under attack while President Donald Trump seeks a staggering 54 percent increase in the military budget.
Medea Benjamin
Medea Benjamin is the co-founder of the peace group CODEPINK and the human right organization Global Exchange. Follow her on twitter at @MedeaBenjamin.

Marta Kos noted that despite Russia's relentless aggression, "Ukrainians continue to pave their path to EU membership."
"Today, we recognized this progress by opening two more negotiating clusters: Internal Market and Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth," she said.
According to Kos, reforms under these clusters will help:
- Prepare for Ukraine's reconstruction;
- Attract investment;
- Modernize the economy;
- Create jobs.
"As one of our frontrunners, we are determined to continue supporting Ukraine and keep this progress going," Kos said.
The European Union is preparing indicative roadmaps for four EU candidate countries: Montenegro, Albania, Moldova, and Ukraine. However, Ukraine's roadmap will differ from the others.
In addition, Ukraine's EU accession process continues to move forward step by step. Hungary has given the green light to negotiations on two more clusters.

articles.summary: US and Europe prepare peace plan to improve post-war state of Ukraine and Russia – The Washington Post  Українська правда
articles.full_text:
The United States and Europe are discussing a joint four-point peace plan that envisages both territorial concessions from Ukraine and Russia, as well as security guarantees and agreements aimed at improving the post-war situation of both countries.
Source: The Washington Post, citing comments from a US official familiar with the negotiations
Quote from The Washington Post: "The package would have four basic components, according to the US official. The message to Putin would be: Don't just end the war with Ukraine. Make an economic and security deal with Europe that would restore stability to the region after an upward spiral of escalation."
Details: The Washington Post explains that the peace plan currently being developed by the US and European nations relies on the principle of "whenever you run into a problem you can't solve, make it bigger".
As part of their diplomatic efforts, US Presidential Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner organised a meeting in Miami on 9 October between representatives from Ukraine, the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany. During the session, they asked the Ukrainians to cease strikes against Russian oil refineries and briefed them on Trump's deal with Russia regarding diesel fuel.
Quote from the official: "We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the post-war situation would be – and then make concessions."
Details: As part of the US-European peace settlement, the US is seeking to put together a package of measures that takes account of the post-war needs of both Ukraine and Russia in such a way as to improve their situation following a territorial compromise that will be unpalatable to both sides.
According to the official, the package will consist of four core components. First will be the reconstruction of Ukraine. The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock are seeking to establish a financial mechanism to rebuild the country's devastated regions, provide assistance to families of fallen and wounded soldiers and restore the shattered economy. Negotiators have already requested detailed cost estimates from Kyiv, along with guarantees that these funds will not be embezzled post-war. The Ukrainian side has not yet provided exact figures but is expected to do so in the coming days.
The second component of the peace settlement will be security guarantees. Ukraine would receive commitments from the US and European nations regarding military intervention in the event of a new Russian attack – which the US official stated is equivalent to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty. They noted that Russia would also enter into agreements with Europe addressing Moscow's security concerns, though the specific terms of this remain unclear.
The third strand will be the economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy agreement. One proposed aspect could be a pipeline transporting Russian oil and gas to Europe, with revenues split between Russia and Ukraine. Such a pipeline could drastically reduce European energy costs, as the official noted.
Aside from granting Russia long-term access to the European energy market, the peace agreement would also define how and when current economic sanctions against Russia will be lifted.
The fourth point of the plan will prove the most unacceptable to both sides, the official claims. It envisages that Russia, which launched the war in the hope of conquering the whole of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the current front line. For Ukraine, this would mean allowing Russia to control occupied territory.
However, a major hurdle for such an agreement is that the "line of control", as negotiators call it, remains fluid due to small daily shifts along the front line.
Background: According to media reports, Witkoff and Kushner informed the Ukrainian delegation at negotiations in Miami that the agreement permitting the export of Russian diesel fuel is part of an effort to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.

articles.title: US and Europe preparing new plan to end war in Ukraine: WP names four key points - Головне в Україні
articles.summary: US and Europe preparing new plan to end war in Ukraine: WP names four key points  Головне в Україні
articles.full_text:
The United States and European countries are gradually shaping a joint proposal to end the war that would offer economic and security incentives to both Ukraine and Russia in exchange for a territorial compromise. According to a US official, the plan consists of four main components: Ukraine’s reconstruction, security guarantees, economic integration, and a ceasefire along the current front line.
The Washington Post columnist David Ignatius writes about the proposal, citing a US official familiar with the negotiations and a European diplomat. The article was published in the Opinions section and describes a plan that is still under discussion.
The talks intensified last Friday during a six-hour meeting in Florida hosted by US presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Ukrainian officials as well as representatives of the United Kingdom, France and Germany took part.
According to the US official, the idea is to broaden the framework of the negotiations and show both sides what the postwar situation could look like.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the source explained.
First pillar — large-scale reconstruction of Ukraine
The first component of a potential agreement would be financing Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction.
According to Ignatius, the World Bank and investment firm BlackRock are working on a mechanism that could raise funds to rebuild devastated regions, restore the economy and support the families of killed and wounded service members.
Negotiators have asked Kyiv to provide detailed estimates of the required costs, as well as assurances that the funds would be protected from misuse after the war ends.
The Ukrainian side is expected to provide the relevant estimates in the coming days, unless the negotiating process collapses.
Second pillar — security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5
The second key component would be long-term security guarantees for Ukraine.
According to the US official, the United States and European countries could commit to responding militarily if Russia attacks Ukraine again. The WP source compared such guarantees in substance to Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty on collective defense.
At the same time, as part of a broader agreement, Russia could also be offered negotiations with European countries over its stated security concerns. It remains unclear what exactly such arrangements might involve.
Third pillar — an energy deal with Russia
Another element of the plan could be the economic integration of Ukraine, Russia and Europe through new energy arrangements.
One option under discussion would involve transporting Russian oil and gas to Europe through a pipeline, with Ukraine and Russia potentially sharing the revenues.
According to the US official, such a scheme could reduce energy costs in Europe while also giving Russia “long-term access to the European energy market.”
A potential peace agreement would also set out the conditions and timetable for the possible lifting of economic sanctions on Russia.
The most difficult issue — territory
The fourth part of the plan would be the most difficult for Kyiv.
Under the framework described by WP, Russia would agree to a ceasefire roughly along the current line of contact.
For Ukraine, this would mean Russia retaining de facto control over the territories it currently occupies, including part of the Donbas. The article does not suggest legal recognition of these territories as Russian.
Another problem is defining the line of control itself, as the situation on the battlefield changes almost every day.
US demands an end to strikes on Russian refineries
The negotiating process has also been complicated by the dispute over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil-refining infrastructure.
According to WP, Kushner and Witkoff again asked the Ukrainian delegation during the Florida meeting to stop attacking Russian refineries. The US official said Washington had raised the issue around six times in recent months amid rising diesel prices.
Ukraine refused, as strikes on refineries have become one of its important tools for putting pressure on the Russian economy. A European diplomat quoted by Ignatius acknowledged that the attacks were having a tangible effect and strengthening Volodymyr Zelensky’s negotiating leverage.
According to the US official, the continuation of the diplomatic mission to Moscow now depends on resolving this issue.
“If Zelensky agrees to halt refinery attacks, we’re back in, and we go to Moscow,” he said.
Europe wants negotiations to continue
Despite European allies’ dissatisfaction with Donald Trump’s agreement involving Russian diesel fuel, according to the WP source, they do not intend to withdraw from the negotiating process.
The key question remains unchanged — whether Vladimir Putin is prepared to agree to ending the war on the proposed terms.
The European diplomat told the newspaper that intelligence available to Western countries does not currently provide grounds to believe that the Russian president is serious about reaching a peace agreement.
Ignatius also stresses in his column that the initiative described remains a diplomatic proposal rather than an agreed peace plan, and that its implementation will depend on whether Kyiv and Moscow are prepared to make compromises.
Earlier, “Glavnoe in Ukraine” reported that during a closed six-hour meeting in Florida, US representatives demanded that the Ukrainian delegation stop strikes on Russian oil refineries and also informed it of Donald Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. The negotiating process subsequently came under threat, while a planned trip to Moscow by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner was put on hold.

articles.title: ECB faces tough decision in October as equities begin to wilt under high interest rates - EUbusiness.com
articles.summary: ECB faces tough decision in October as equities begin to wilt under high interest rates  EUbusiness.com
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank’s monetary policy committee will meet on October 29 to decide whether to hike rates for a second successive month or keep them unchanged. Expectations are high for the latter, with prediction market platforms pointing to a 91% chance that there will be no hike in October.
That seems to be the most popular view of the markets ahead of this month’s key Central Bank decisions. Yet, rising inflation continues to challenge that view.
In September, euro area inflation rose to 3.8%, compared to 3.2% in August, largely impacted by rising energy prices, which represented an 18.8% rise in the harmonized index of consumer prices, rising from 14.3% in August. Eurostat attributed the sharp rise in energy CPI to the conflict in the Middle East.
The ECB hiked rates in September when annual inflation in August stood at just 3.2%, so it makes sense to think the committee may continue the current tightening cycle in October.
So what could prevent a rate hike in October?
The ECB’s September rate hike affected EU markets differently. Each country has its own bond market, which means an ECB rate can result in higher sovereign bond yields in one country and lower yields in another, due to different economic circumstances.
For instance, the 10-year French government bond (OAT) recently hit a new all-time high of 4.9%, which analysts have attributed to concerns over France’s Fiscal outlook and draft budget.
On the other hand, German government bonds are being viewed by investors as a haven, with the 10-year Bund yield dropping to 3.4%.
The spread between the sovereign bonds is more than 1.4%, the widest since 2011, during the eurozone crisis. This level of fiscal fragmentation is hurting EU equity markets, even though some continue to demonstrate resilience. The French CAC 40 index is down nearly 10% since August 10, while the German DAX 30 index is down 4% since the start of September.
The current pullbacks come on the back of significant rallies, with the CAC 40 gaining more than 13% between March 20th and August 10th, while the DAX 30 rallied nearly 19% between March 20th and August 28th. Overall, CAC 40 is down 3.75% this year, while DAX 30 is up 2.65%.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, commenting on the relative strength EU equities demonstrated before the latest pullback: “European indices contain many multinational companies whose earnings depend more heavily on global demand than domestic European GDP. This helps explain why European equities have remained relatively resilient despite the deteriorating sovereign backdrop,” she shared in a bond markets analysis a week ago.
The seasonally adjusted GDP in the euro area grew by 0.6% in Q2 2026, on the back of a 0% growth rate in Q1, according to estimates published by Eurostat. Q2’s growth rate is the highest the euro area GDP has grown in a quarter since the second quarter of 2022.
Different EU member states experience varying growth rates, with Ireland, which posted a 10.2% growth rate, becoming an outlier in the mix. Only five other member states managed to post a growth rate of at least 1%, with several, including France, remaining flat.
Therefore, while rising inflation often calls for tightening, an assessment of the euro area economic situation, coupled with equity prices that are beginning to wilt under the pressure of higher interest rates, means the European Central Bank faces a tough decision on October 29, when the committee sits down to decide whether to continue tightening or keep rates unchanged.

articles.title: The ECB’s options in dealing with France’s fiscal woes - ING Think
articles.summary: The ECB’s options in dealing with France’s fiscal woes  ING Think
articles.full_text:
The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high. However, a further deterioration in France's situation could eventually force the ECB to demonstrate whether its 'whatever it takes' commitment still holds
The ECB’s most powerful tools are the ones it has never used. They are the tools that the ECB developed after Mario Draghi’s ‘whatever it takes’ speech. Tools that showed ‘whatever it takes’ was something markets could believe in. The Outright Monetary Transactions programme during the euro crisis and the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) after the pandemic both shared the same objective: to enable potentially unlimited purchases of government bonds if needed.
Political and fiscal woes in France and the widening of the French spread have now raised the question of whether the ECB could intervene through TPI, which allows it to purchase securities issued by member states whose financing conditions have deteriorated for reasons not justified by country-specific fundamentals. However, before activating it, the Governing Council considers a cumulative set of criteria to determine whether the countries concerned are pursuing sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies. In practice, this includes compliance with the EU fiscal framework, which would, at a minimum, require the proposed French budget to be fully adopted.
The ECB has nevertheless left itself some discretion, stating that the intervention criteria “will be dynamically adjusted to the unfolding risks and conditions to be addressed”. This brings back memories of the famous “because it’s France” by former European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker. Generally speaking, the ECB will be in a difficult position: intervening too quickly in support of France may be viewed unfavourably by other member states and interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules. That argues strongly against early intervention. Also, don’t forget that the leadership changes at the ECB over the next months (Schnabel, Lane, Lagarde) could also affect how the ECB views TPI.
Given the challenges of justifying the activation of TPI at present, we expect the ECB to adopt a three-pronged approach to address the French crisis.
The first line of defence is a more dovish approach to policy rates. As bond markets are currently taking over the ECB’s job of inserting a more restrictive monetary stance on the economy, there is less need for the ECB to hike rates aggressively, or to hike rates at all. In fact, the ECB has already started to prepare this option, as ECB president Christine Lagarde recently noted that “while growth has been resilient, since our last meeting long-term interest rates have risen notably, which will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise".
The second line of defence would be a covert return to bond purchases. The ECB could instead pause quantitative tightening temporarily and reinvest maturing bonds in its portfolio “flexibly”, sending a positive signal to bond markets. This had already happened during the Covid period.
Last but not least, and in our view, the ultimate option in the case of more contagion in eurozone bond markets, the ECB would eventually trigger TPI. As long as France remains non-compliant with the European fiscal rules, the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France.
All in all, the current French situation is simply not enough for the ECB to trigger TPI. There are other ways to tackle any unwarranted impact from higher bond yields on the broader eurozone economy. However, a further escalation could eventually force the ECB to prove whether its 'whatever it takes' commitment still holds.

articles.title: Why have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms? - France 24
articles.summary: Why have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms?  France 24The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial  The GuardianUkraine is being thrown to the wolves  The TelegraphHardly his finest hour  The EconomistGift for Putin as fears grow that Trump is turning the screws on Ukraine  CNN
articles.full_text:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” on Wednesday after access was seemingly restricted to US intelligence and Space X satellite services, raising new questions about US commitment to Ukraine. With Trump under pressure over rising fuel prices, is the White House hoping criticism of Kyiv can help shift the blame?
For two nights this week the Ukrainian military were stunned by apparent restrictions on its access to Starshield – the satellite internet service owned by billionaire Elon Musk – and claimed that US intelligence warnings had also been cut off, leaving civilians especially vulnerable to ballistic missile attacks.
The restrictions occurred amid simmering tensions between Washington and Kyiv and sparked concerns that the US was pulling back on intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after ratcheting up rhetoric against Zelensky.
Read moreWhat is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Zelensky said in an interview during a visit to the UK on Wednesday that he felt betrayed by the US.
Connectivity to Starshield – which is a SpaceX satellite internet service reserved for military use – was restored on Thursday, Ukrainian authorities said.
But much damage was already done. As well as multiple casualties from Russia’s overnight attacks, the restrictions revived fears in Kyiv that the US is an essential but increasingly unreliable ally.
Zelensky called for “honesty” on Thursday after Musk denied responsibility for the lapse – saying the Pentagon was responsible for any restrictions to the satellite service – and US President Donald Trump denied that the US intelligence-sharing policy had changed.

Going ‘too far’
But fears of a change in the US commitment to Ukraine have not come out of the blue.
Trump last week announced a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, reversing years of US sanctions on Moscow to ensure “lower prices for Americans” who have hit by an ongoing cost of living crisis.
Zelensky criticised the deal as a “weak decision” to which Trump responded on Saturday by saying that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
He also also claimed that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries were the reason for rising diesel prices in the US.
Meanwhile, Musk – who has recently renewed his alliance with Trump since a public fallout back in June – has started speaking out against Ukraine’s attacks on Russian data centres.
“Elon Musk came out specifically to say that that was going “too far” so it’s no surprise that just a couple of days later this change has happened,” said David Galbreath, professor of War and Technology at the University of Bath, in an interview on Wednesday with FRANCE 24.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Midterm pressure
Musk and Trump’s reconciliation comes as the tech billionaire has become the biggest Republican donor ahead of November’s US midterm elections, spending $245 million to back key candidates.
The upcoming vote – which will define the next two years of Trump’s presidency – may be one reason for the changing attitude towards Ukraine.
“Republicans are facing poor electoral prospects due to high energy prices and affordability pressures arising from Iran war,” said Majda Ruge, senior policy fellow for the US at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “These pressures explain why President Trump has become particularly hostile towards Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries just weeks before the midterms.”
Similarly, Trump’s surprise announcing of an energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow was an attempt to demonstrate “a foreign-policy success” to voters, Ruge said.
“Whether reality aligns with claims of this foreign policy success is less relevant. The story of the president as a dealmaker and his foreign policy ‘wins’ is not intended for the audience that follows the international affairs closely,” she said.
Dramatic interventions related to international oil supply are similarly “to demonstrate that Trump is doing something about the cost-of-living problem”, added Jonathan Monton, associate professor in political science and director of the International Public Policy Programme at University College London.
“There's very little that he can do practically to change the real cost-of-living issues anytime between now and the midterms, so these kinds of gestures are all he has.”
‘Targets in a shooting gallery’
Although Musk has said any restrictions on Starshield were decided by the US military, he doubled down on his criticism of the Ukrainian president.
“Time for Zelensky to go,” he wrote on Thursday in a post on X.
Both Trump and Musk “understand significantly” how disruptions to Starlink would affect Ukraine, Galbreath said.
The satellite internet service enables mid-range drone flights without which the Ukrainian military would unlikely be able to continue its frontline pushback in the east or use interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s high-speed Shahed drones.
Read moreHybrid warfare: The threat of Russia looms over the Mediterranean
“Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals, and schools like targets in a shooting gallery,” Ukrainian human rights lawyer and Nobel Peace Prize winner Oleksandra Matviichuk wrote on social media.
“Let me be blunt: the blood of Ukrainian children will be on the hands of the owner and the entire team of this American company,” she added with reference to SpaceX.
The reasons for Musk’s recent decision to become an outspoken critic of Ukraine’s military strategy are unclear.
So entrenched has his technology become in the Ukrainian military apparatus that in August Musk was awarded Ukraine’s Order of Freedom for his "outstanding personal merits" in protecting human life and strengthening ties with the United States.
“He's putting up big money to help the Republican side in the midterms,” said Monton. “So maybe he just genuinely agrees with Trump that alleviating these supply constraints would help the Republicans, and this is his way of pressuring Zelensky into going along with that. But it's very hard to tell.”
Zelensky, meanwhile, indicated he is unlikely to bow to the pressure. Ukraine initially complied with Trump’s impromptu "energy ceasefire" last week – even as Zelensky said the announcement of the agreement was “news to [him]” and Russia continued striking Ukrainian infrastructure.
But on Thursday he signalled a change of heart: "The block [on attacking refineries] is out,” he told the Financial Times. “We're done."

articles.title: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast - The Guardian
articles.summary: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast  The GuardianSeven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast  BBCRussia suspected of striking two tankers in Nato waters  Financial TimesBlack Sea drone attacks enter NATO country’s territorial waters for first time  Ars TechnicaNATO allies to meet over Black Sea drone attacks on shipping  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
Seven sailors are missing after drones struck two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns on a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.
A Nato military source told Reuters the drones that had hit the Wine Trader and the Yara J came from Russia. “The drones that caused the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the source said.
Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, described the situation in the Black Sea as serious. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk,” he wrote on X. “Seafarers killed, injured and missing very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”
His statement followed a meeting with Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, and Nato’s secretary-general, Mark Rutte, on Thursday, where they agreed “to strengthen our defences in the Black Sea”, Dan said.
Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
A Nato official said the issue would be discussed at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council next week.
The missing crew were from the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged tanker travelling from Tunisia to Romania. All crew on the Yara J, which was struck just inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday, were safe.
Similar incidents in recent weeks have raised fears that the zone is becoming another front in Russia’s war on Ukraine.
Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether Russia was responsible.
Romania shares a 614km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. The country has experienced frequent drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including a daytime encroachment last November that led Nato to scramble fighter jets.
EU leaders were already concerned about drone strikes on merchant ships off the coast of Bulgaria. On Tuesday, drone strikes on two ships off the coast of Bulgaria prompted emergency rescue operations, with 11 crew member from the HS Dignity, a cargo ship sailing under a Guinea-Bissau flag, still missing.
On another ship, the Ukrainian-operated Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries. The crew reported that the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.
“The results of this attack favour Russia. However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russians,” Radev said after arriving in Brussels for an EU summit on Thursday.
At least 23 sailors have been reported missing or killed after attacks on commercial shipping near the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania in the past 10 days, according to Reuters.
Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on Ukraine’s Black Sea infrastructure, forcing Kyiv to turn to Danube river ports and Black Sea routes off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria to export its grain, sunflower oil and other products.
According to a draft summit declaration, EU leaders will say that attacks against civilian shipping, including “member state-flagged vessels, such as the recent attacks in Bulgaria’s and Romania’s exclusive economic zones in the Black Sea, are unacceptable and constitute a serious violation of international and maritime law”.

articles.title: France Cyberattack Spoils Food in 400 Supermarkets - logos-pres.md
articles.summary: France Cyberattack Spoils Food in 400 Supermarkets  logos-pres.md
articles.full_text:
According to BFMTV, a total of around 400 retail outlets have been affected by the cybercriminals: 300 shops belonging to the Intermarché and Netto chains, fewer than a hundred Coopérative U shops, as well as Leclerc hypermarkets and a number of independent shops. Experts estimate that the total damage to the retail sector will amount to several million euros.
Large-scale equipment failure
The attackers found a vulnerability in outdated versions of software produced by the Danish engineering giant Danfoss, which manufactures industrial refrigeration control systems. Having breached the system, the hackers took control and forcibly activated the automatic defrost function.
Under normal operating conditions, this process lasts no more than two hours a day to remove ice build-up. However, the hackers triggered continuous heating of the equipment, setting the target temperature to 50°C. The equipment continued to heat up throughout the night.
“Instead of keeping things cold, the display cabinets turned into ovens. When staff arrived at work in the morning and opened the cold stores, a veritable wave of heat burst out,” said representatives of the affected retail chains.
As a result, dairy products, juices, fresh meat, fish and frozen ready meals were rendered completely unusable. In some shops, only the freezers were affected; however, in those where the incident began earlier, staff had to completely clear out and dispose of the entire contents of the fresh food sections.
The damage to individual supermarkets is estimated at tens and hundreds of thousands of euros. For example, the Leclerc store in the commune of Vaslon lost goods worth 220,000 euros, whilst the nearby Intermarché lost a further 50,000 euros.
Shoppers across France have been faced with half-empty shelves. Shop management are posting emergency notices on the doors of switched-off fridges, whilst shoppers are having to rethink their diets, buying only long-life goods.
A threat to Europe’s food security
At the request of the French Prime Minister, the National Agency for the Security of Information Systems has joined the investigation. Experts have already confirmed the existence of a vulnerability in Danfoss software and have contacted the Danish developer, as well as companies specialising in the maintenance of industrial refrigeration systems.
French cyber security services are urgently liaising with their counterparts in other European countries, as Danfoss software is widely used throughout the EU, and the incident in France may prove to be merely the first wave of a large-scale attack on European logistics and retail.

BEIJING — The European Union is pushing to lift sanctions on a Chinese company in order to rescue a German semiconductor parts maker pushed to the brink of collapse by China's rare earth restrictions.
At high-level trade talks held in Beijing on the 8th and 9th of this month, the EU and China discussed lifting trade restrictions imposed on a Chinese company suspected of supporting Russia's war in exchange for China lifting sanctions on Germany's Schindelhauser Materials, Bloomberg reported on the 14th. Schindelhauser is a small and midsize company specializing in precision semiconductor manufacturing and advanced coatings, and it supplies parts to ASML, the world's largest maker of semiconductor lithography equipment.
The EU had earlier sanctioned the Chinese company on the grounds that it supplied key components used in weapons production to Russia. China retaliated in July by adding 14 European companies, including Schindelhauser, to its export control list. Schindelhauser depends entirely on supplies of Chinese rare earths and critical minerals and is said to face the risk of shutting down within months if the Chinese sanctions remain in place.
Analysts say the targeting of a little-known German small business shows how meticulously China is moving to weaponize its resources. Over the past year and a half, China has used licensing requirements for critical minerals and rare earths to collect wide-ranging information on global supply chains. It requires foreign companies to submit detailed materials, including information on end customers, how Chinese raw materials are used and photographs of final products. Observers say this allowed China to identify weak links in the supply chain of Europe's semiconductor industry and strike them with precision.
Bloomberg noted that German companies are handing over trade secrets to China while the German government cannot obtain even a comparable level of information, adding that the more serious problem is that Berlin has yet to devise a strategy to address this gap in economic intelligence-gathering capability.

articles.full_text:
Reports have emerged that the United States proposed unfreezing a portion of frozen Russian government assets to European partners in an effort to restart stalled peace negotiations for Ukraine.
Citing four sources familiar with the matter, the Financial Times (FT) reported on the 14th local time that a U.S. delegation met with officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union (EU), and NATO in Miami last week to pitch the proposal.
During the meeting, the U.S. side presented several concrete mechanisms for lifting the freeze, including creating a new special-purpose financial entity to transfer the unfrozen Russian assets under the supervision of the U.S. government.
European delegations reportedly expressed strong opposition to the initiative, which was allegedly spearheaded by White House Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
A U.S. government official explained that the plan was put forward as part of a comprehensive peace agreement, adding that specific procedures on how the assets would be unfrozen and where they would be allocated are still under discussion.
The FT reported that the U.S. proposal sent shockwaves through European capitals and the Ukrainian government, fueling doubts about Washington's sincerity and whether its approach to pressuring Russia to halt its invasion has diverged sharply from Europe's.
Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Western allies froze approximately 260 billion euros (about 391 trillion won at current exchange rates) in Russian state assets, the vast majority of which are held within the EU.
While Ukraine secured 45 billion euros (about 68 trillion won) in loans from Group of Seven (G7) nations backed by interest generated from these frozen assets, European governments have been reluctant to touch the principal assets themselves due to legal risks.
EU leaders agreed late last year to use the assets to fund Ukraine's reconstruction costs if Russia fails to pay war reparations.
Consequently, unfreezing the Russian assets would require unanimous consent from all 27 EU member states, a scenario considered highly unlikely in reality.
Ukraine and some European countries have consistently maintained that these assets should be used directly to support Ukraine.
Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said through Russian state media on the 14th that "we will mobilize all legal means, trials, and judicial procedures to recover the confiscated assets."

Under the ongoing U.S. force posture and basing review, outdated military bases, fuel supply chains and agreements governing the stationing of American troops in Europe will be scrutinized.

articles.title: "Relaxation of Internal Combustion Engine Vehicle Regulations and Preference for European-Made Cars" — EU Defends Against Market Infiltration by Chinese Automotive Industry, Impacting Overseas Complete Vehicle Manufacturers - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: "Relaxation of Internal Combustion Engine Vehicle Regulations and Preference for European-Made Cars" — EU Defends Against Market Infiltration by Chinese Automotive Industry, Impacting Overseas Complete Vehicle Manufacturers  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
France and Germany pushing for further relaxation of EU internal combustion engine vehicle phase-out regulations
Acceleration of Chinese electric and hybrid vehicles' market infiltration in Europe, increased trade barriers
Increased burdens on other overseas automakers such as Tesla, Toyota, and Nissan
France and Germany are pushing for the European Union (EU) to ease regulations phasing out internal combustion engine vehicles. Amid the rapidly growing presence of Chinese-made electric and hybrid vehicles in the European market, the plan aims to reduce the transition burden on domestic vehicle manufacturers while strengthening EU production and procurement requirements to protect the industrial base. Additionally, Europe is accelerating the preparation of further countermeasures such as the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). These regulations are posing challenges not only to Chinese companies but also to many overseas vehicle manufacturers' European business strategies.
Discussions on easing internal combustion engine vehicle regulations by France and Germany
According to the Financial Times (FT) on the 13th (local time), French President Emmanuel Macron said on the 12th at the Paris Motor Show, "An agreement on EU automotive policy is imminent," and "We are finalizing an agreement with Germany to allow Europe to move forward." In these negotiations, Germany is demanding a relaxation of the 2030 emission reduction targets applied to car manufacturers, and in particular, is pursuing easing the EU's ban on sales of new internal combustion engine vehicles set to apply from 2035. The main point is to allow up to 10% of new car sales to be internal combustion engine vehicles after 2035. The agreement is also expected to exclude obligations to use low-carbon fuels or low-carbon materials in internal combustion engine vehicles.
France appears to be securing support through cooperation with Germany to focus public subsidies and procurement contracts in core technology fields such as electric vehicles and batteries on EU-based manufacturers. This measure aims to strengthen the European automotive supply chain and production base. However, changes to EU regulations cannot be made through agreements between only the two countries; amending related laws requires approval from the council involving EU member states and the European Parliament. Particularly, the expansion of allowed sales of new internal combustion engine vehicles significantly relaxes existing EU climate policy goals, so considerable controversy may arise during future discussions.
Chinese electric vehicles expanding influence in Europe
The market views these moves by European countries as a form of check against Chinese automotive companies. Over the past several years, Chinese companies have rapidly expanded their influence in the European automotive market, led by electric vehicles. According to the European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA), 20% of pure electric vehicles sold in the EU last year were manufactured in China. Market researcher JATO Dynamics also reported that the market share of Chinese automotive brands in Europe rose from 2.7% in the first half of 2024 to 5.1% in the first half of last year, with sales increasing by 91% during the same period.
The EU has consistently erected trade barriers to curb this rapid rise of China. Since 2023, the EU has conducted an anti-subsidy investigation on Chinese electric vehicles for about a year, and in July 2024, imposed provisional anti-dumping duties on Chinese EVs, finding that Chinese government subsidies distorted competition in the internal market. This was the first large-scale trade sanction on Chinese electric vehicles. Subsequently, in October of the same year, the EU finalized, with member state approval, additional anti-dumping duties of up to 35.3% per company on Chinese-made electric vehicles. Specifically, BYD faced a 17.0% duty, Geely 18.8%, Shanghai Automotive Industry Corporation (SAIC) 35.3%, and Tesla vehicles produced at the Shanghai plant were subject to a 7.8% tariff. These tariffs are added on top of the existing 10% import tariff on automobiles, applied from October 30, 2024, for a duration of five years.
Strong hybrid vehicle offensive
As EU trade barriers increased, China expanded sales of hybrid vehicles, which have relatively lower tariff burdens, penetrating the local market. According to China's General Administration of Customs, exports of hybrid vehicles from China to the 27 EU member states totaled $7.72 billion in the first half of this year, three times the $2.57 billion during the same period last year. Compared to the annual export value of $869 million in 2021, this is about nine times larger. The FT also analyzed that Chinese automakers' market share in the EU plug-in hybrid market jumped from 2% in 2024 to 25% in the first half of this year.
In response, the European Commission asked China to voluntarily reduce exports of hybrid vehicles to Europe and lower market share, but China refused. After continued conflicts, the two sides recently agreed to cap annual imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 units. This measure is expected to take effect as early as early December, with the annual allowed volume increasing by 6% each year. Furthermore, the import cap applied to China will not be lower than caps applied to other exporting countries.
Table 1. EU countermeasures against Chinese-made automobiles
| Category | Main contents | 
|---|---|
| Pure Electric Vehicles | Impose company-specific anti-dumping duties on Chinese electric vehicles in addition to existing import tariffs | 
| Hybrid Vehicles | Limit annual import volumes of Chinese hybrid vehicles to the EU, with allowable volumes gradually increasing each year | 
Tesla faces European regulations
Industry attention focuses on that these European moves to protect domestic industries are affecting not only Chinese companies but also foreign automakers overall. A representative case is American electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla. Tesla recently changed the name of its autonomous driving technology in Europe from 'Full Self-Driving Supervised (FSD)' to 'Tesla Assisted Driving.' This was a response to Germany's Federal Ministry of Transport's statement on the 6th that the FSD designation could cause misunderstandings about the actual technological level. German authorities pointed out that the system is not a fully autonomous driving technology that performs all driving tasks, but a driver assistance system supporting some driving tasks such as acceleration, braking, and steering. Drivers must continuously monitor the surroundings and be able to take direct control of the vehicle immediately if necessary during system operation.
Regulatory barriers were prominent even during the process of introducing this driver assistance system across the EU. Earlier, after about 18 months of safety testing, Tesla received FSD system approval in April from the Dutch vehicle certification authority (RDW), but this did not immediately lead to commercial authorization throughout the EU. In the EU, when new vehicle technologies do not fully comply with existing safety regulations, a separate exemption approval process must be followed under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation (EU 2018/858). For Tesla to offer this technology throughout the EU, the Dutch authorities must submit an application to the European Commission for EU-wide approval, followed by a vote in a relevant committee comprising member states.
Japanese automakers also on alert
Japanese automakers remain concerned about the EU's proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). This bill focuses on protecting production bases of European companies and expanding demand for European-made products in response to low-cost competition from non-EU countries such as China. It targets key strategic industries including automotive, steel, cement, aluminum, and batteries. In the automotive sector, the bill suggests applying EU production and parts procurement requirements to electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles receiving public procurement and some subsidies and tax benefits. According to the Commission's draft, such vehicles must generally be finally assembled within the EU, and the local procurement ratio of vehicle parts, excluding batteries, must exceed 70% based on retail price. Separate local production requirements have also been set for battery cells and key drive components.
Toyota, a leading Japanese automaker, produced approximately 80% of its vehicles sold in Europe last year within the European region, but this figure includes production in the UK and Turkey, which are non-EU countries. On June 6, Yoshihiro Nakata, CEO of Toyota Europe, urged that key partner countries such as the UK, Japan, and Turkey be included in the IAA’s list of recognized EU-origin areas. Nissan faces a similar issue. According to a March report by The Guardian, Nissan reportedly warned the UK government that if the UK is excluded from the IAA's EU-origin recognition scope, the Sunderland plant's closure might need to be considered. The Sunderland plant directly employs about 6,000 people and is the UK's largest automotive production facility with an annual capacity of up to 600,000 vehicles.

articles.title: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears - The Guardian
articles.summary: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears  The GuardianA trial over one of the biggest acts of sabotage in decades is getting underway. Here’s a refresher  CNNGermany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines  BBCGerman prosecutors accuse Ukraine of Nord Stream sabotage  Financial TimesUkrainian on trial in Germany over 'war crime' bombing of Nord Stream pipeline  Sky New...
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that, acting on the order of state authorities, laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, a court has heard.
On the opening day of his trial in the German city of Hamburg, Serhii Kuznetsov, who was a special forces officer with the Ukrainian military at the time of the pipeline attacks in 2022, was accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.
He appeared in court on Wednesday dressed in a grey suit, white shirt and black tie and flanked by his lawyers. Kuznetsov saluted as he entered the courtroom. He and his legal team listened in silence for 10 minutes as the federal prosecutor general read out the indictment, which was simultaneously translated into Ukrainian.
Kuznetsov, 50, is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres in the Baltic Sea close to the Danish island of Bornholm.
He is believed to have had six accomplices – four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain – who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives.
Kuznetsov and his country deny any involvement in the attacks.
Kuznetsov’s lawyers argued that the trial should not be taking place at all, telling the court that the defendant, who they said had been held almost entirely in solitary confinement for 11 months, was being treated “like a pawn on a chessboard”.
They stressed his inability to defend himself in the conventional manner due to his role as an army officer, which they said forbade him from speaking. It meant he was having to defend himself “with his hands tied”. They also disputed the accusation that the attack was sabotage of civilian infrastructure, saying the pipelines were “a weapon in the hand of the Russians”.
The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany.
The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in response to the Kremlin’s aggression. They exposed the dependence of Europe – and in particular Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime.
Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully.
In July, German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved.
Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 on a family holiday in Italy, with Italian police reporting that he surrendered without resistance. He had been travelling on a false passport. He was extradited to Germany last November after legal efforts to prevent this failed.
Another suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, an air conditioner installer and hobby diver, was arrested on a European warrant in northern Croatia in August. He is fighting his extradition to Germany, having applied for asylum in Croatia. He denies any role in the sabotage.
Aware of how potentially incendiary the trial could be, with Ukraine in effect in the dock for a crime committed against its ally – and one of its staunchest wartime supporters – the German government has declined to comment on the proceedings.
On Wednesday, a group of protesters gathered outside the court holding Ukrainian flags and placards. One of them, a Ukrainian man in exile in Germany, said: “It’s a scandal that a Ukrainian is being accused of a war crime here today, when Russia is constantly committing war crimes in Ukraine.”
The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis.
The pro-Ukraine protesters who turned out on Wednesday were just a few feet away from a group of supporters of the far-left BSW party, which echoes the AfD’s stance on Russia and would also like to see the pipelines reinstated. They were holding placards demanding a parliamentary inquiry to investigate any political motives behind the Nord Stream attack.
Nord Stream was already a controversial subject before the attack. Vladimir Putin and the then German chancellor, Gerhard Schröder, managed to bypass Ukraine as a transit country with Nord Stream 1. After Schröder left the chancellery, Putin appointed him as chair of the supervisory board of the company Nord Stream AG. Schröder was seen last week attending Putin’s birthday celebration.
A request by the Russians to participate as co-plaintiffs in the Hamburg trial was rejected by the court. The company Gazprom, which owns the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, had argued its right to do so due to what it referred to as the severe economic consequences resulting from the attack. The court argued that while repair costs of the pipelines would be high, it would not be economically impossible to restore them.
According to reports, Kuznetsov, whose military ID indicates he was in active service at the time the pipelines were blown up, is expected to maintain his right to remain silent during the trial.
His legal team is expected to produce affidavits from two of his military superiors to support the argument that he is prohibited from revealing details of his actions as a soldier.
He is reported to have allegedly taken his orders from a man who is considered to be the mastermind behind the attack and is one of those who have sworn in his favour.
The trial will resume on 27 October.
Sixteen trial days have been scheduled at Hamburg’s Hanseatic higher regional court up to and including 17 December, with further hearings likely in January.

articles.title: India–EU FTA could strengthen Czech investment and manufacturing ties - Maritime Gateway
articles.summary: India–EU FTA could strengthen Czech investment and manufacturing ties  Maritime Gateway
articles.full_text:
Summary
Czech companies are seeking joint ventures, investment and technology partnerships in India, with the India–EU trade agreement expected to support deeper commercial ties. Czech minister Karel Havlíček outlined opportunities in engineering, construction, energy and transport during a business forum in New Delhi. The agreement is not yet in force.
The Czech delegation looks beyond export sales.
The India–EU FTA could create opportunities for Czech investment and joint ventures in India, according to Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Addressing the CII-organized India–Czech Republic Business Forum in New Delhi on 12 October, Havlíček said Czech businesses were interested in establishing partnerships and investing locally alongside their export activities.
He identified construction, energy, transport and research and development as areas for cooperation. He also highlighted Czechia’s engineering capabilities, including aircraft manufacturing.
The minister linked the delegation’s interest in local partnerships with India’s manufacturing strategy. His remarks describe prospective business opportunities, rather than a quantified investment commitment or a confirmed portfolio of new projects.
Business mission covers three Indian centres
The forum forms part of a Czech business mission scheduled for 12–15 October, covering Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.
Ahead of the visit, the Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade said the mission would support companies entering the Indian market and those seeking to expand existing operations.
The programme also included a planned roundtable with Invest India focused on developing bilateral investment opportunities. Direct business contacts and meetings were identified as important elements of the delegation’s approach.
The mission places the minister’s comments within a broader effort to develop commercial relationships. For participating companies, the immediate focus is identifying partners and market opportunities while the trade agreement progresses through its approval process.
The visit’s stated objectives combine market entry, business expansion and investment cooperation, extending the engagement beyond the promotion of finished-product exports alone.
Negotiations concluded, implementation still pending
India and the European Union concluded FTA negotiations on 27 January 2026. The European Commission subsequently put forward a proposal for a Council decision authorising signature.
Negotiating an agreement, signing it and bringing it into force are separate stages. The EU process requires the relevant Council decisions and European Parliament consent, while India must also complete its approval requirements.
Consequently, the agreement’s tariff preferences should be understood as forthcoming provisions, rather than benefits already available to shipments.
The talks began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and resumed in 2022. Separate negotiations on investment protection and geographical indications were also launched alongside the renewed FTA process.
That distinction is relevant to the investment discussion: the trade agreement and the separate investment protection negotiations address related but different aspects of the commercial relationship.
Industrial tariff reductions underpin the opportunity
The negotiated agreement envisages eliminating or reducing tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports to India by value. The European Commission estimates eventual annual duty savings of approximately €4 billion for European products.
Industrial goods feature prominently. Tariffs on machinery, chemicals and pharmaceuticals are to be mostly eliminated, while automobile and component provisions include phased reductions.
These changes provide a commercial backdrop to Czech interest in engineering and industrial cooperation. Lower trade barriers could support cross-border equipment and component supply, although individual benefits will depend on product coverage and implementation schedules.
The agreement also includes provisions on intellectual property and services, including maritime transport. Such commitments extend its scope beyond merchandise tariffs and could support businesses combining technology, equipment and services.
The Commission’s projections concern the overall EU–India relationship; they do not establish a specific increase in Czech exports or investment.
Indian exporters also stand to gain
The agreement provides reciprocal opportunities for Indian businesses. India’s commerce ministry says more than 99% of Indian exports by trade value will gain preferential access to the EU.
Engineering goods, textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, marine products and other labour-intensive sectors are among the areas identified for improved access.
The framework also covers rules of origin, customs and trade facilitation, regulatory cooperation and technical barriers to trade. These provisions matter to manufacturers seeking to build supply relationships across the two markets.
For ports, freight forwarders and logistics providers, any resulting expansion in industrial trade could create additional demand for cargo movement. Its scale will depend on implementation and actual business decisions.
The Czech delegation’s engagement therefore represents an effort to develop partnerships ahead of the agreement’s application, with investment and manufacturing cooperation central to the discussion.
FAQs
What opportunities are Czech companies exploring?
Joint ventures, investment and cooperation in engineering, construction, energy, transport and research and development.
Who outlined these opportunities?
Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Is the India–EU FTA already in force?
No. Negotiations have concluded, but the agreement must complete signature and approval procedures before taking effect.
Were specific Czech investment commitments announced?
The reported remarks did not provide a quantified investment package.
How could Indian exporters benefit?
The agreement envisages preferential EU market access across a broad range of Indian exports, subject to its provisions and implementation.

Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet functionality has been fully restored, a source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Thursday, a day after the crucial service was throttled at speeds of over 100 miles per hour.
The source said the Defense Ministry would continue to seek clarification on the reasons for Wednesday's disruption of the military-grade version of SpaceX's internet service, which affected drone missions across the frontl ine.
“As of now, Starshield’s work in motion has resumed and continues, we record this in reports from units,” the Ukrinform news agency quoted its Defense Ministry source as saying.
Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday that the functioning of Starlink’s military-grade service Starshield had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defense.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear but followed a souring of relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, after Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
Zelensky has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their U.S. counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
EU leaders are set to urge Volodymyr Zelenskyy to tone down his public criticism of Donald Trump, amid concerns that the Ukrainian president’s increasingly blunt remarks risk further damaging already strained relations between Washington and Kyiv.
In an interview with the FT on Wednesday, Zelenskyy criticised the US leader’s recent diesel deal with Russia, condemned a “dangerous” withdrawal of US intelligence support and said Trump had an affinity for autocrats and the ultra-rich.
That blunt assessment startled EU leaders who will meet Zelenskyy in Brussels on Friday and urge him to moderate his rhetoric during closed-door talks, three officials briefed on the summit preparations told the FT.
“It might be true, but it doesn’t always need to be said out loud,” said one of the officials. The message from the 27 leaders will be empathetic but firm, the officials added.
Trump’s announcement he had struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to stop striking Russia’s refineries and US proposals to unfreeze Russian state assets have led to the worst crisis since Trump gave Zelenskyy a public dressing-down in the Oval Office last year.
The breakdown in relations puts Kyiv’s European allies, who also rely on Washington for critical defence and intelligence support, in a bind.
“We want to continue helping Ukraine. And I am pleased that Zelenskyy will be with us tomorrow,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters on Thursday.
“We must do everything in our power to support Ukraine . . . it remains my firm conviction that we are not merely defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity; we are defending the political order of Europe, which is currently being put under intense pressure from Russia in every respect,” he added.
The US no longer provides financial aid to Ukraine and only supplies weapons paid for by Kyiv and its European allies. But Washington’s intelligence is critical to the country’s ability to defend against Moscow’s attacks and strike targets in Russia.
During previous flare-ups in his rocky relationship with Trump, European leaders have sought to comfort Zelenskyy and travelled to Washington to convince the US leader to remain supportive of his Ukrainian counterpart.
But many are planning to adopt a slightly more critical tone towards Zelenskyy on Friday morning, the officials said, while still expressing support — given the fragility of transatlantic relations and Russia’s relentless attacks on Ukraine.
“We have to continue our engagement with the United States because we’ve had moments in the past when there were challenges and difficulties in respect of this and it was retrieved by good outreach and engagement with the United States,” said Micheál Martin, Ireland’s prime minister, when asked about Trump’s stance on the war on Thursday. “I’ve no doubt that will continue.”
“We definitely have different approaches [compared with the US] to this war,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, when asked about the US-Ukraine tension. “We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop this war, not the victim. Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s call for a new Ukrainian leader, saying any successor would continue defending Ukraine and that choosing a president was a decision for Ukrainians.
Speaking on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Zelensky rejected the suggestion that his departure would resolve the obstacles to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
He said a future president, whether a man or a woman, would still have a responsibility to protect the country.
“I am sure that a new man or woman will defend our country, because this is our home,” Zelensky said.
“How can you do otherwise?”
His response challenged Trump’s argument that a change in Ukraine’s leadership could produce an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump said on Saturday, Oct. 10 that Ukraine needed a new president capable of reaching a deal, accusing Zelensky of passing up opportunities to end the war.
Morgan put Trump’s comments directly to Zelensky, telling him: “He wants you gone.”
Zelensky responded that Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory had begun before he took office. When he became president, Crimea and parts of the Donbas region were already occupied, as his predecessor had also confronted Russia.
Zelensky’s argument was that Ukraine’s resistance reflected the country’s interests rather than the position of one president. According to him, a successor might defend Ukraine better or worse, but would nevertheless defend it, rejecting the idea that foreign figures should determine who holds office.
His removal, he said, would be “a decision for our people, not Trump, not Musk, not anyone else.”
Asked whether he intended to resign, Zelensky answered: “No, of course not. This is my responsibility.”
He said holding a presidential election was currently nearly impossible because Russian attacks continued every hour.
On Monday, Oct. 12, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed that Trump had suggested Ukraine choose a new president because Zelensky was unwilling to make the decisions needed to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“Trump said that, in his opinion, it is time for a new president,” Peskov said.
“Why? Because the president of Ukraine must make very responsible and very difficult decisions to stop this war.”
Peskov accused Zelensky of failing to demonstrate the political will to take those steps.
“Either Zelensky takes on that responsibility and demonstrates that political will, or he does not,” he said. “So far, he has not.”
